title: From Manipur to the World: The Air India Siblings Who Share a Career in the Skies
excerpt: Cabin crew siblings Wahengbam Sureiya and Rohit Singh navigate the same rosters, long-haul flights, and airport standbys — discovering that the person who best understands the demands of aviation is family.
body:
• Wahengbam Sureiya and Rohit Singh, cabin crew siblings from Imphal, Manipur, both work for Air India — Sureiya since 2014 and Rohit following a decade later.
  • Sureiya was the first in her family to pursue aviation, drawn by the opportunity to travel and the variety of the profession.
  • Growing up listening to his sister's flight stories, Rohit was inspired to follow the same career path and joined Air India as cabin crew.
  • The siblings say that working for the same airline — navigating shared rosters, long-haul flights, and layovers — has brought them closer than ever.

The First to Fly

In 2014, Wahengbam Sureiya became the first person in her family in Imphal, Manipur, to pursue a career in aviation. Drawn by the chance to travel the world, meet people from different backgrounds, and work in a profession where no two days are alike, she joined Air India as cabin crew and quickly found her calling.

Back home in Imphal, eight years younger, her brother Rohit Singh was paying attention.

He grew up listening to stories from her flights — the destinations she visited, the experiences she brought home, the rhythms of life at 35,000 feet. What started as a younger sibling's admiration gradually sharpened into a career decision.

"She was the first one in our family to dream about a career in aviation. Seeing her become cabin crew and travel to different parts of the world really inspired me. I loved hearing about her experiences, and eventually I decided to follow in her footsteps."

— Rohit Singh, Air India cabin crew

From Siblings to Colleagues

Years later, Rohit joined Air India as cabin crew, starting a journey remarkably similar to the one his sister had begun a decade earlier. Today, both wear the Air India uniform. But sharing a profession, they say, is only part of what makes their situation special.

Working for the same airline has brought them even closer than growing up in the same household did. They navigate the same rosters, handle the same long-haul flights, and understand the particular demands of airport standbys and layovers in ways that colleagues without a sibling in the business cannot.

The person who best understands the exhaustion of a red-eye turnaround, the stress of a difficult passenger, or the particular loneliness of being far from home during holidays is often the person who has known them since childhood.

A Story From India's Northeast

The siblings' story is also one about India's Northeast — a region that has long been underrepresented in the country's aviation workforce and in mainstream media coverage of the industry. Manipur, connected to the rest of India by a narrow corridor and bordered by Myanmar, has produced athletes, artists, and military personnel in numbers that belie its small population. Aviation professionals from the state are less commonly profiled.

Air India's own newsroom featured the siblings' story as part of the airline's broader narrative of transformation. Under the Tata Group's ownership since early 2022, Air India has been expanding its fleet, upgrading service standards, and recruiting crew from across the country as it works to reclaim its position as India's flagship international carrier.

What It Means

For diaspora travelers who fly Air India on routes connecting India to North America, Europe, and beyond, the siblings are part of the crew that makes those journeys work. Their story is a small but telling reminder that behind the uniforms are individual paths — shaped by family, by geography, and by the particular pull of a career that literally takes you places.
